title: How do `ClassOption.WEAK` vs `STRONG` affect hidden-class garbage collection, and what does `NESTMATE` enable?
shortTitle: `ClassOption.WEAK` vs `STRONG` for hidden-class GC, and what `NESTMATE` enables
topicTitle: How do `ClassOption.WEAK` vs `STRONG` affect hidden-class garbage collection

s1_definition.profdef: When you define a hidden class with `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass`, the `ClassOption` values control its lifecycle and access. By default a hidden class is weakly reachable relative to its defining loader, so it can be garbage collected and unloaded as soon as it becomes unreachable. The `STRONG` option ties the hidden class's lifetime to its defining class loader, so it is only unloaded when that loader is unloaded. The `NESTMATE` option makes the hidden class a nestmate of the lookup class, granting it access to the lookup class's private members and vice versa. (Note: `WEAK` is the conceptual default behaviour; the explicit option provided is `STRONG`, and omitting it gives the weak, independently-unloadable behaviour.)
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India generates temporary helper rules. A STRONG helper is like an employee given a permanent contract tied to their whole department — they stay as long as the department exists. A WEAK helper is like a contractor hired for a single task who is let go the moment the task is done and nobody needs them, so the bank does not keep paying for idle staff. NESTMATE is like giving the helper a family membership in the department so they can open the private filing cabinets the regular staff use, and the regular staff can open theirs — shared private access within the family.
s1_definition.oneliner: STRONG keeps a hidden class alive as long as its loader lives, WEAK (the default) lets it be unloaded as soon as it is unreachable, and NESTMATE grants shared private-member access between the hidden class and its host.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When you define a hidden class with `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass`, the `ClassOption` values control its lifecycle and access. By default a hidden class is weakly reachable relative to its defining loader, so it can be garbage collected and unloaded as soon as it becomes unreachable. The `STRONG` option ties the hidden class's lifetime to its defining class loader, so it is only unloaded when that loader is unloaded. The `NESTMATE` option makes the hidden class a nestmate of the lookup class, granting it access to the lookup class's private members and vice versa. (Note: `WEAK` is the conceptual default behaviour; the explicit option provided is `STRONG`, and omitting it gives the weak, independently-unloadable behaviour.)

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India generates temporary helper rules. A STRONG helper is like an employee given a permanent contract tied to their whole department — they stay as long as the department exists. A WEAK helper is like a contractor hired for a single task who is let go the moment the task is done and nobody needs them, so the bank does not keep paying for idle staff. NESTMATE is like giving the helper a family membership in the department so they can open the private filing cabinets the regular staff use, and the regular staff can open theirs — shared private access within the family.

**One line to remember:** STRONG keeps a hidden class alive as long as its loader lives, WEAK (the default) lets it be unloaded as soon as it is unreachable, and NESTMATE grants shared private-member access between the hidden class and its host.

sections.s2_technical:
Normal classes are reachable from their defining class loader, so a normal class is only unloaded when its entire class loader becomes unreachable and is collected. Hidden classes change this. By **default** (no `STRONG` option), a hidden class is only **weakly** held by the runtime relative to the loader, meaning that once there are no strong references to the hidden class's `Class` object or its instances, the hidden class can be **garbage collected and unloaded on its own**, even though the defining loader stays alive. This is the memory win: frameworks generating many short-lived classes do not accumulate them in metaspace.

The **`STRONG`** option changes this lifecycle. A strong hidden class is kept alive as long as its **defining class loader** is alive, exactly like a normal class. You choose `STRONG` when the hidden class must persist for the lifetime of the application or the loader, for example a generated class that is cached and reused many times, where repeated unloading and regeneration would waste CPU. The trade-off is that strong hidden classes do not give you the independent-unloading memory benefit; they live and die with the loader.

The conceptual **`WEAK`** behaviour, which is the default when you do not pass `STRONG`, is the opposite: the hidden class is eligible for unloading as soon as it is unreachable. You rely on this when each generated class is used briefly and then discarded, such as a per-request expression evaluator or a per-trade rule, where keeping thousands of them alive would exhaust metaspace. The practical rule is: use the default weak behaviour for throwaway generated classes, and use `STRONG` only for long-lived, cached generated classes.

The **`NESTMATE`** option is about access, not lifecycle. The Java nest concept lets classes in the same nest access each other's private members directly. When you pass `NESTMATE`, the hidden class becomes a nestmate of the **lookup class** that defined it, so the hidden class can read and call the lookup class's private fields and methods, and the lookup class can access the hidden class's private members too. This is essential for generated code that must touch private internals of its host — for instance, the lambda metafactory generates a hidden class that needs access to the captured private state of the enclosing class. Without `NESTMATE`, the generated hidden class would be denied access to those private members and would need public or package-level entry points.

A senior nuance is that these options **compose**: you can pass both `STRONG` and `NESTMATE`, giving a long-lived hidden class with private access to its host, which is typical for a cached proxy that must call private host methods. Another nuance is that the weak-by-default lifecycle interacts with **metaspace** management, so in a banking microservice that generates rule classes per request, relying on the default avoids a slow metaspace leak that would eventually trigger `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`. A final nuance is that `NESTMATE` is what makes hidden classes a clean replacement for the old Unsafe host-class mechanism, which also gave generated classes access to a host's internals but through an unsupported path; `NESTMATE` formalises that access via the specified nest-based rules.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India generates a short-lived validation class for each incoming transfer request. Thousands of transfers arrive per minute, and if every generated class stayed in metaspace forever the service would eventually crash with a metaspace out-of-memory error. We need each generated class to be unloaded as soon as the request finishes. This is the default weak lifecycle of a hidden class.

Problem 2 — The bank also caches one generated, reused interest-calculation class for the whole life of the service because regenerating it per call would waste CPU. This one must not be unloaded while the service runs. This is the `STRONG` option.

Problem 3 — Both generated classes must read private configuration held inside the host engine, such as a private fee rate. Normally a separate class cannot touch private members, so we pass `NESTMATE` to make the generated hidden class a nestmate of the host, granting shared private access.

In the mini-project we build a `RuleEngine` host with a private field, define a weak hidden class for per-request validation, define a strong hidden class for the cached calculator, use `NESTMATE` so both can read the host's private rate, and log the lifecycle and access behaviour.

The code contains: a `RuleEngine` host, calls to `defineHiddenClass` with different `ClassOption` combinations, and a `main` demonstrating weak unloading, strong retention, and nestmate access.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/hiddenopt/OptionsDemo.java

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.hiddenopt.OptionsDemo

# Observe class unloading of WEAK hidden classes

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a `RuleEngine` with a private fee rate of 0.1%, used to define one weak validator class, one strong calculator class, and to compute a fee of 0.1% on 1,000,000.

Step 1 — `main` builds a `RuleEngine` whose `feeRate` field is private. This private state is what we will reach from hidden classes using `NESTMATE`.

Step 2 — `defineWeakValidator` defines a hidden class without the `STRONG` option, so it uses the default weak lifecycle. We log that it is hidden and note it will be unloaded once unreachable. If you run with class-unload logging you can see it unloaded after it goes out of scope.

Step 3 — `defineStrongCalculator` defines a hidden class with the `STRONG` option, so it is tied to the loader's lifetime and will not be independently unloaded. This is the cached, reused class case.

Step 4 — `computeFeeViaHidden` defines a `NESTMATE` hidden class and instantiates it with the engine. Because it is a nestmate, the hidden class can read the host's private fee rate through the package-private accessor. It computes 0.1% of 1,000,000, which is 1,000.00, using `BigDecimal` with half-up rounding.

Step 5 — The fee is logged. The weak validator becomes eligible for unloading immediately, the strong calculator stays, and the nestmate access succeeded, demonstrating all three options together.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] WEAK validator hidden=true (will unload when unreachable)
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] STRONG calculator hidden=true (kept alive with its loader)
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Fee computed by NESTMATE hidden class using host private rate = Rs.1000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  RuleEngine(feeRate=0.001 PRIVATE)
    │
    ├─ defineWeakValidator()
    │    lookup.defineHiddenClass(bytes, true, NESTMATE)   ← no STRONG
    │    → WEAK hidden class ──(unreachable)──▶ UNLOADED (metaspace freed)
    │
    ├─ defineStrongCalculator()
    │    lookup.defineHiddenClass(bytes, true, STRONG, NESTMATE)
    │    → STRONG hidden class ──▶ lives until LOADER unloaded
    │
    └─ computeFeeViaHidden(1,000,000)
         lookup.defineHiddenClass(bytes, true, NESTMATE)
         new CalculatorImpl(engine)
         └─ NESTMATE access → engine.feeRate() reads PRIVATE 0.001
            1,000,000 × 0.001 = 1000.00
         ▼
       return Rs.1000.00
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ClassOption Semantics ═══

  ┌─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ (default / WEAK): unload when unreachable, loader stays alive │
  │ STRONG:  lifetime tied to defining class loader               │
  │ NESTMATE: shared private access with the lookup (host) class  │
  │ compose: STRONG + NESTMATE = long-lived + private host access │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ RuleEngine (host / lookup class)          │
  │ - feeRate: BigDecimal   (PRIVATE)         │
  │ + feeRate(): BigDecimal (pkg accessor)    │
  │ + defineWeakValidator(): Class  (WEAK)    │
  │ + defineStrongCalculator(): Class (STRONG)│
  │ + computeFeeViaHidden(amt): BigDecimal    │
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                  │ NESTMATE grants access
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CalculatorImpl (hidden, nestmate)         │
  │ - engine: RuleEngine                      │
  │ + calculate(amt): amt × engine.feeRate()  │  reads host PRIVATE rate
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Lifecycle:
    WEAK:   DEFINED → USED → UNREACHABLE → UNLOADED
    STRONG: DEFINED → USED → (stays) → unloaded only with loader

  Call Chain:
    1. defineWeakValidator() → NESTMATE, no STRONG
    2. defineStrongCalculator() → STRONG + NESTMATE
    3. computeFeeViaHidden(1,000,000)
    4.   new CalculatorImpl(engine)
    5.   engine.feeRate() → 0.001 (private, allowed via NESTMATE)
    6.   → 1000.00
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I define a hidden class with defineHiddenClass, the class options control its lifecycle and access. By default, with no STRONG option, a hidden class is only weakly reachable relative to its defining loader, which means it can be garbage collected and unloaded on its own as soon as nothing strongly references its Class object or instances, even though the loader is still alive. This is the big memory benefit for frameworks that generate many short-lived classes.

The STRONG option changes that lifecycle by tying the hidden class to the lifetime of its defining class loader, exactly like a normal class, so it is only unloaded when the loader is unloaded. I choose STRONG when a generated class is cached and reused many times and regenerating it would waste CPU. I rely on the default weak behaviour when each generated class is used briefly and discarded, because keeping thousands alive would exhaust metaspace. In my banking project I use the weak default for a validator generated per transfer request, so it unloads after the request, and STRONG for a single cached interest calculator that lives for the whole service.

NESTMATE is about access rather than lifecycle. Java's nest concept lets classes in the same nest read each other's private members directly. When I pass NESTMATE, the hidden class becomes a nestmate of the lookup class that defined it, so the generated class can read and call the host's private fields and methods, and the host can access the hidden class's privates too. This is exactly what the JDK's own lambda metafactory needs, because the generated class must touch captured private state of its enclosing class.

In my rule engine the host holds a private fee rate, and my generated calculator is defined as a NESTMATE so it can read that private rate and compute the fee. The options also compose, so I can pass both STRONG and NESTMATE to get a long-lived cached generated class that still has private access to its host, which is typical for a cached proxy. So in one sentence I explain it as: STRONG keeps the class alive with its loader, the weak default lets it unload as soon as it is unreachable, and NESTMATE gives the generated class shared private access to its host.
